newsitem.title: ITALY: EU leaders hail 40 years of peace.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders hail 40 years of peace.

text.p: European Union dignitaries toasted 40 years of integration and peace among members on Tuesday and pledged not to allow the opportunities presented by the fall of communism to slip by them.
"Life for the Union begins at 40," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said at a commemorative ceremony to mark the signing of the Treaty of Rome on March 25, 1957.
The treaty created the European Economic Community among West Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg.
Now standing at 15 countries, the bloc is poised to expand into former Communist east Europe.

"Europe today has a historic chance to bring the whole continent together," European Commission President Jacques Santer said in a speech to dignitaries gathered in the same chamber of Rome's city hall where the 1957 treaty was signed.
"Let us take inspiration...from the birth of the European Economic Community and build the Europe of the 21st century, a Europe for Europeans with Europeans," he said.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said Europe should be proud of what it had achieved over the past 40 years but that more needed to be done.
"There is no room for individual actions...Europe is our destiny," he said, urging fellow members to strive for deeper integration.
He said economic growth had to be accompanied by steps to reduce the EU's unemployment queues.
"When unemployment exceeds 10 percent as it does on the EU average, we are facing an unacceptable waste of human resources," Prodi said.
"It would be impossible to explain to our citizens that the worl'd greatest economic bloc was not capable of responding to their principal concern," he said.
Turning aside criticisms that the EU is too often divided, Santer said there had always been differences of opinions as the bloc had grown from six to 15.
"But the essence of our Union is to seek, while respecting the dignity and diversity of each of our member states, an answer that preserves all our interests," he said.
"What unites us is much more important than what divides us," he said.
